profiles.name: Francis Mel Madden
profiles.description: Francis Melvin "Mel" Madden, a Boston native, was ordained a Franciscan priest in 1965 and founded Liberty Village, a Jersey City drug-treatment center, in 1967. By 1971 he had married, had two children, and worked as training director for New Jersey's drug-education program, from which he was suspended without pay after his arrest. He was severed from the main trial and his charges were dismissed after the May 1973 acquittals.
profiles.finding: Camden 28 priest and Liberty Village founder identified in film press kit; no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Margaret Inness
profiles.description: Margaret Mary Inness (November 6, 1944 – August 22, 2021) was a Boston native, a Regis College graduate, a former novice with the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur, and a special-education teacher completing a master's degree at Boston College at the time of the Camden 28 indictment. Tried as one of the seventeen and acquitted on May 20, 1973, she went on to teach in Boston public schools for more than thirty years. Her married name was Margaret Inness Galvani. She died in Savannah, Georgia on August 22, 2021 — fifty years to the day after the raid.
profiles.finding: NARA arrest record; unrelated Nova Scotia Margaret Inness and Margaret Sharp Inness rejected. Follow married-name Margaret Inness Galvani obituary (2021).

profiles.name: Barry Musi

profiles.name: Michael Giocondo
profiles.description: Michael Giocondo was a former Franciscan brother (12 years, stationed in Costa Rica and Washington DC), age 42 at indictment. Worked in Camden where he founded El Centro, an inner-city service for Spanish speakers, and co-founded the bilingual newspaper GAP. It was Giocondo who first brought Bob Hardy into the group. Acquitted in 1973.

profiles.name: Sarah Tosi
profiles.description: Sarah Tosi, from Ho-Ho-Kus, New Jersey, was twenty at the Camden 28 indictment. A 1969 graduate of Immaculate Heart Academy and National Honor Society president, she had been a district coordinator in the 1968 McCarthy campaign, attended Wellesley College, and was active in Boston's Paulist Center and in Dorchester community work. Later accounts identify her among the drivers supporting the Camden operation rather than those inside the draft-board office. She was severed from the main trial and her charges were dismissed after the May 1973 acquittals.
profiles.finding: Camden press kit and spouse memoir; no verified image.

profiles.name: Milo Billman
profiles.description: Rev. Milo Billman, a Lutheran minister ordained in 1958, was the only Protestant clergyman among the Camden 28. He had worked with Appalachian communities near Cincinnati, helped develop an antipoverty organization in Columbus, and served as outreach director of Camden's EPOC program. He was severed from the main trial and his charges were dismissed after the May 1973 acquittals.

profiles.name: Chuma
profiles.description: Chuma was identified by the Republic of New Afrika as one of the RNA-11 arrested during the August 18, 1971 FBI and police raid on the organization’s provisional-government residence in Jackson, Mississippi. profiles.name: Karim Njabafudi
profiles.description:
Karim Hekima Oman Wadu Njabafudi — born Larry Jackson in New Orleans, also recorded as Karim and "Brother Black" — was a citizen of the Republic of New Afrika and, at about fifteen, the youngest of the RNA-11 arrested in the August 18, 1971 FBI and Jackson police raid on the RNA Provisional Government residence at 1148 Lewis Street in Jackson, Mississippi. A contemporary 1971 booklet preserved by the Amistad Research Center gives his full adopted name and identifies him as Larry Jackson, and federal court records identify him as "Larry Jackson, a/k/a Karim and Brother Black."

At about 6:30 that morning, agents and police holding a fugitive warrant for another man and misdemeanor warrants for three people — one of them a warrant for "Larry, last name unknown", later identified as him, over an alleged assault on a newspaper reporter at RNA headquarters — surrounded the house and fired tear gas. In the gun battle that followed, Jackson police lieutenant William L. Skinner was killed and another officer and an FBI agent were wounded; the seven occupants then surrendered. Court testimony attributed the fatal shot to Hekima Ana, not to Njabafudi, who reportedly told agents he had fired a .30-06 rifle from the west side of the house. Mississippi convicted him of murder as an aider and abettor, under a statute treating an accessory before the fact as a principal.

Tried from September 22, 1972 — venue moved from Hinds County to Lauderdale County — he was convicted and sentenced to life on September 25, 1972, expressly in the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman. The Mississippi Supreme Court affirmed on March 24, 1975 and denied rehearing on May 12, 1975. He was released in November 1979.

The federal court dismissed him from the adult federal prosecution of the RNA defendants because he was a juvenile who had not waived his rights under the Federal Juvenile Delinquency Act; the government said it would proceed against him separately as a juvenile, but no judgment proving that prosecution or any federal sentence has been located, so claims of a federal fifteen-year term are unresolved. His birth date is likewise unresolved: the Mississippi Supreme Court put his age at fifteen and two-thirds on the day of the raid, implying a birth around December 1955, while a federal footnote called him sixteen; the year is entered at circa precision and no exact date is inferred.

He is not the Larry Jackson of the November 1970 New Orleans Black Panther raid — that alias belonged to John England Morris Jr., who has his own record in this database.

profiles.finding: Right On 1972 trial reporting and African World remain archive leads; no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Jayma Abdoo
profiles.description: Jayma A. Abdoo (1951 – August 2006) was the youngest documented member of the Camden 28, twenty at the 1971 indictment. A graduate of Immaculate Heart Academy in Bergen County, she had worked in Eugene McCarthy's 1968 presidential campaign and was a children's librarian. She was severed from the main trial and her charges were dismissed after the May 1973 acquittals. She later graduated with honors from Columbia University and became an assistant dean at Barnard College. She died of cancer in August 2006.
profiles.finding: Michelle Nickerson additional resources and Columbia obituary establish Camden identity; photo unverified.

profiles.name: Edward Murphy
profiles.description: Edward Murphy was a Jesuit priest and NYC native, age 34 at indictment; entered the Society of Jesus in 1955, ordained 1968, taught Classics and Theology. A member of the New York 8, he ran a GI coffeehouse near Fort Devens, MA, worked as a draft counselor, and was a national coordinator of the Harrisburg Defense Committee. Acquitted in 1973.

profiles.name: Eugene Dixon
profiles.description: Eugene "Gene" Dixon was a Camden resident, father of four, and a longtime supervisor for a Philadelphia automotive company, thirty-seven at the Camden 28 indictment. He was active in Catholic religious education and the PTA and was known as a poet. He was severed from the main trial and his charges were dismissed after the May 1973 acquittals. He continued writing poetry and books after retirement.

profiles.name: Martha Shemeley
profiles.description: Martha Lee Shemeley was a Camden social worker, a former diocesan teacher, a Seton Hall psychology graduate and a published Catholic writer who lectured on the role of women in the church and on the "underground church". She was thirty-four at the Camden 28 indictment and the mother of a ten-year-old. She was severed from the main trial and her charges were dismissed after the May 1973 acquittals. Contemporary press used the spelling Shemeley; Shemely appears in secondary accounts. A genealogical record suggesting a birth in March 1936 under the maiden name Martha Lee Haley is a probable but unverified match, so it is noted here and not entered.
profiles.finding: Camden press kit; genealogy matches not independently linked.

profiles.name: Anita Ricci
profiles.description: Anita Ricci, a Philadelphia native, was twenty-two at the Camden 28 indictment. She had graduated near the top of her class at St. Maria Goretti High School, won a scholarship to the University of Pennsylvania, studied sociology at Temple University, and worked at Philadelphia's Resistance Book Store. Unlike her co-defendants she entered a guilty plea to a lesser charge before the seventeen-person trial; the exact disposition and any sentence remain unresolved, and later accounts that fold her into the statement that all twenty-eight were acquitted or dismissed are wrong. Her father's February 2007 obituary refers to her as his late daughter, establishing only that she died before that date.
profiles.finding: Camden press kit and Notre Dame CPF April1973; no verified image.

profiles.name: Charles Koen
profiles.description: The Reverend Charles Koen was national chairman of the Black United Front of Cairo, Illinois, a hub of the long Black freedom struggle in that southern-Illinois town. His imprisonment stemmed from a September 1968 incident in which he and Brother Leon Dent were stopped over a defective brake light, arrested, and beaten by eight officers at the police station (Koen suffered head lacerations and broken bones in his hands); Koen was then charged with assault on a police officer and convicted. After his appeal was denied in 1971 he was sent to the St. Louis Workhouse to serve a six-month sentence, where he conducted a water fast in protest that left his weight down from 170 to 110 pounds before Judge David McMullan granted him parole. Documented in The Black Panther (September 25, 1971).

profiles.finding: NYU Cairo photo collection, Illinois broadsides, Panther Dec19 1970 and Militant3444 captioned images pending inspection; UPI resale photo rights unresolved.

profiles.name: Bill Himmelbauer

profiles.name: Gary Lawton
profiles.description: Gary Lawton was a Black community activist in Riverside, California, one of two men charged with the April 1971 murder of two Riverside police officers — a prosecution his supporters, organized as the Riverside Political Prisoners Defense Committee, denounced as a frame-up. Lawton was the central defendant, tried again and again over the killings; his wife, Charlene, was among the committee members injured in a March 1974 Riverside police attack on a defense-committee picket line. By 1974 Lawton and Gardner had been tried twice, with both trials ending in hung juries (reportedly 11 to 1 for acquittal), and a third trial was pending; the case never produced a conviction. Documented in The Black Panther (April 13, 1974).
profiles.finding: Smithsonian Free Gary Lawton object and Highway13 May1974; distinguish art from actual photo before use.

profiles.name: Samuel Bridges
profiles.description: Samuel “Sam” Bridges was a former Stanford Hospital worker whose firing helped provoke the April 1971 hospital sit-in. Police stopped Bridges and Black Liberation Front member Chris Laury while they were driving to Ukiah on May 16, 1971. A contemporary account says officers beat both men and accused them of offenses involving a visible .45-caliber pistol, marijuana and an open wine bottle. Both pleaded not guilty. The available record does not establish an overnight booking, a release date or the disposition of the charges.

profiles.name: Chris Laury
profiles.description: Chris Laury was a member of the Black Liberation Front in East Palo Alto, California. Police arrested him on May 7, 1971 over the alleged beating of Stanford Hospital clerk Mary Jane Schmidt during a hospital-workers’ struggle and set bail at $12,500. Laury maintained that he had been misidentified. His trial began in late November 1971, and a jury found Laury and co-defendant Leo Bazile not guilty of every charge. Police also stopped and arrested Laury with Samuel Bridges on May 16, 1971 while they were driving to Ukiah; both pleaded not guilty to the resulting weapons, marijuana and open-container accusations. No exact custody interval has been established for either arrest.

profiles.name: David Hofstetter
profiles.description: David Hofstetter was one of four University of Wisconsin–Madison activists arrested on May 4, 1971 following a disruptive protest in the Gordon Commons dining hall during the Residence Halls Student Labor Organization (RHSLO) strike — a roughly two-week campaign for recognition, a contract, and improved conditions for student residence-hall and food-service workers. Tried in the summer of 1971, all four remained free pending appeal as of December 2, 1971; whether the sentence was ultimately served is not documented in the available reporting. Hofstetter was convicted of disorderly conduct and resisting arrest and sentenced to six months.

profiles.name: Charles Hopkins
profiles.description:
Charles Hopkins — who adopted the name Mansa Musa after reading Malcolm X's writings on African history, rejecting the surname inherited from his enslavers — was arrested in 1971 at the age of 19 after a 7-Eleven robbery in Prince George's County, Maryland in which a customer, who turned out to be an off-duty park police officer, was shot. He was given a life sentence. He would later discover that the police officers handling the case were members of a unit subsequently exposed as a "death squad" that fabricated evidence and suppressed exculpatory information in multiple cases.

Hopkins served **48 years, 9 months, and 5 days** in the Maryland prison system, cycling through six or seven institutions including Hagerstown Correctional Institution, Jessup Correctional Institution, the Maryland Correctional Training Center, and four and a half years in a supermax facility. Inside, he became a central organizer of the **Maryland Penitentiary Intercommunal Survival Committee (PISC)**, a Black Panther–aligned prisoner formation that ran educational programs, literacy instruction, and prisoner-support work. He led organizing among prisoners across the country to engage the United Nations on U.S. prison conditions, corresponding with political prisoners including Anthony Bottom (Jalil Muntaqim) and Sundiata Acoli.

He was released on **December 5, 2019** on conditional release. Since then he has co-hosted **"Rattling The Bars"** on The Real News Network — first alongside fellow former Black Panther political prisoner Marshall "Eddie" Conway until Conway's death in 2023, and continuing the show since — and works with reentry programs including Voices for a Second Chance. He remains a prominent public voice on prison abolition, prisoner solidarity, and the connection between the carceral system and the labor struggle.
profiles.finding: Real News author page explicitly bridges Charles Hopkins to Mansa Musa and matching release history; interview portrait/video lead retained. Unrelated educator and military namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: Grady Fuller
profiles.description: Grady Fuller was a twenty-two-year-old member of the National Committee to Combat Fascism in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. Police arrested Fuller and fifteen-year-old Cary Coe on January 12, 1971 after accusing them of stealing meat from a delivery truck, an accusation the organization described as a pretext for raids on the Black community and its office. Fuller’s bail was set at $7,000. On March 19, 1973 he pleaded no contest to misdemeanor larceny and two misdemeanor assault charges. The court imposed ninety days and credited him with twelve days already served. The available record establishes those twelve days of confinement but does not identify their exact endpoints or show whether he served any balance of the sentence.

profiles.name: Charles Parker
profiles.description:
Charles Parker was a young civil rights and antiwar activist in Charlotte during an era when Black political organizing in the South was frequently met with aggressive surveillance, infiltration, and prosecution. His activism is most closely associated with the same local milieu of organizers targeted in the early 1970s.

Parker was one of the “Charlotte Three,” arrested in late 1971 and convicted in 1972 for the 1968 arson that destroyed Lazy B Stables. He received a 10-year sentence, the shortest among the three defendants, but the case still became a widely discussed civil-rights controversy. In 1979, Governor Hunt commuted the sentences, and Parker was released.

profiles.name: Susan Stern
profiles.description:
Susan Stern was an antiwar activist and one of the Seattle Seven. During the December 14, 1970 contempt proceedings she continued speaking in support of her co-defendants after the judge ordered her to stop.

The prosecution concerned the February 17, 1970 antiwar demonstration in Seattle. Judge George Boldt declared a mistrial and imposed summary contempt sentences. On November 18, 1971, the Ninth Circuit reversed the contempt judgments because the procedure and factual certifications were inadequate. Further contempt proceedings produced reduced sentences; the original conspiracy prosecution ended in 1973. The original sentences do not establish the actual total time served.
profiles.finding: HistoryLink Seattle Seven and UW gallery; film/author portraits need exact identity verification.
